While Israel is fiercely resisting these terms, Iran and its proxy Hezbollah are insisting on them – something that has already led to more bloodshed.

At about the same time as The Telegraph was in Majdal Zoun on Friday, a four-man IDF tank crew was killed by a suspected Hezbollah drone or rocket attack in Kfar Tebnit, 22 miles to the north-east.

Israel responded with 150 air strikes that it said had killed “dozens of terrorists” across Lebanon.

Kfar Tebnit, like Majdal Zoun, also conceals a large Hezbollah tunnel network, according to Israel media.

The flare-up was seized upon by Israel’s ruling coalition government which faces an election in October and is under significant pressure over the failure of the Iran war.

In Bürgenstock, Switzerland, US and Iranian negotiators, including Mr Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as well as Mr Vance, began 60 days of negotiations.

“The question before us now is how much more can we accomplish together? Can we turn over a new leaf?” Mr Vance asked.

“Can we change relations in the Middle East permanently, or do we go back to doing things the old way, which is not our preference, but is certainly very much something that can happen,” he added.

But just as the negotiations threaten Israel’s freedom of action, they have also sapped the credibility of the Lebanese government, experts say.

Michael Young of the Carnegie Middle East Centre in Beirut told The Telegraph that the Lebanese government, already weak, was being undermined by both the Israelis and the Iranians, reducing its ability to disarm Hezbollah.

“The Lebanese are paying the price for both sides,” he said. “The Israelis are not that interested in giving them anything that can strengthen the credibility of the Lebanese state, and nor do the Iranians have any interest in giving anything that may make the Lebanese state more credible.”

Although the US’s return to diplomacy has been welcomed by most leaders around the world, primarily because it has reopened the Strait of Hormuz, few believe the issue of the Israel-Lebanon conflict will be resolved any time soon.

The two sides were again trading blows on Saturday. Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, knows he would face electoral oblivion were he to pull the IDF out of Lebanon before the October elections in Israel.

Meanwhile in Lebanon, Iran is tightening its grip on Hezbollah.

“Since the assassination of Hassan Nasrallah back in September 2024, the Iranians have got a tighter control, they’ve been involved with the reorganisation of the Islamic resistance, the military component of Hezbollah, and we’ve seen that visibly over the last three or four months,” said Mr Blanford.

And on both sides people are dying. More than 100 IDF soldiers have been killed in the Israeli-Hezbollah conflict since Oct 7, 2023, and nearly 50 civilians. On the Lebanese side, nearly 4,000 people have lost their lives since March 2 this year alone.

“Trump’s Epic Failure With Iran Will Bring About Catastrophic Consequences”

🔤🔤🔤🔤➖

Trump’s deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for lifting sanctions on Iran is getting strong pushback from Senate Republicans who warn that giving Iran’s theocratic regime access to billions of dollars in economic relief would be a major “blunder.”

Some Republicans are warning that the likely outcome of the more than 100-day conflict is not worth the cost to the nation: the lives of 13 American service members and more than $100 billion spent.

“Ronald Reagan is rolling over in his grave,” fumed Sen. Bill Cassidy in a social media post, calling the war and its outcome the “worst foreign policy blunder in decades.”

“Iran’s nuclear ambitions were not curbed, and they have learned that threatening the Strait of Hormuz works and will undoubtedly leverage it in the future. Now, Iran gets to build brand-new infrastructure under this deal,” he wrote on the social platform X.

“Now, 13 Americans are dead, families have paid billions at the pump, sanctions will be lifted, and the bombing has stopped,” he continued.

Most concerning to some Senate GOP critics is that the deal will immediately lift sanctions on Iranian oil exports and may lead to the unfreezing of Iranian assets around the world.

“History teaches that giving billions of dollars to theocratic lunatics who want to murder us is not a good idea. I think the president is receiving some very poor advice on this deal,” said Sen. Ted Cruz. 

The deal leaves open the future of Iran’s nuclear program and does not clearly prohibit Iran from levying tolls on the Strait of Hormuz at some point in the future, according to senators who reviewed the deal.

It also leaves open the future of Iran’s missile program, which remains robust even after weeks of American and Israeli bombardment, according to intelligence estimates.  

A classified CIA assessment estimated that Iran still had 70 percent of its prewar missile stockpile and 75 percent of its mobile missile launchers, according to a report by The Washington Post.

Sen. John Cornyn said the lack of significant Iranian concessions on its nuclear program, its weapons arsenal and its long-standing practice of funding militant proxies throughout the Middle East raises serious concerns. 

He pointed out the deal doesn’t prevent Iran from continuing to enrich uranium or toll the strait, and “it gives them a lot of money they can use to fund their proxies.”

The agreement would only guarantee that Iran does not impose tolls on the Strait of Hormuz for a period of 60 days. After that time, Iran will negotiate with Oman to define the future administration of, and maritime services through, the strait.

Sen. Thom Tillis said it’s hard to argue that Trump’s decision to order joint missile strikes with Israel against Iran in late February produced an outcome to justify the cost in lives and munitions.

Tillis said the deal appears weak “on its face.”

“You got to do the balance of accounts: a hundred billion roughly, maybe more, spent today; 13 dead, 365 wounded, injured; our partners in the Middle East bombed, they’ve had casualties. There’s got to be a lot of return on that,” Tillis said, summing up the cost of the conflict.

He said Trump appears to have fallen well short of his objectives at the start of the war.

“We set out by saying we were going to drive down to zero their nuclear capability. Now we’re equivocating on that. We said that we were not going to make the mistake that Obama did by sending them a plane full of cash. I got to reconcile the numbers there,” he said.

“There’s a lot of work to be done to convince me that we’re on the right path,” Tillis added.

According to CryptoQuant CEO Ki Young Ju, the days of altcoins surging just because Bitcoin is climbing might be coming to an end.

In past market cycles, money would naturally flow from BTC into altcoins, sparking widespread altseason rallies. But that pattern seems to be weakening.

Today’s market is much more discerning. Liquidity is clustering around fewer assets, institutions are largely prioritizing Bitcoin, and many altcoins are finding it tough to draw in substantial investment—even as BTC performs strongly.

This doesn’t mean altseasons are extinct—but the era where nearly every token rode the Bitcoin wave could be over.

The new reality may come down to this:

📈 Bitcoin rises.  
❌ Not all altcoins follow.

Moving forward, narratives, fundamentals, and genuine user demand could become more crucial than ever.
